messages.content: 1st the close up of this image will be very nice as if the vessel is leaking into a bucket, but now the bucket is a bucket of muscle. So you are saying retroperitoneals are rounded the fat right? This will be a very nice image. Umm. But how did, how did they accident occur? He fell. The ribs punctured. Something tore through the Renault lottery. It's a rental vessel. OK. OK.

Exactly. The mechanism is a **deceleration shear injury**. The kidney is tethered at the renal hilum; the rib fractures from the fall lacerate the renal parenchyma or avulse the renal artery or vein. That torn vessel spills blood into the **retroperitoneal space** — a confined, fat-filled bucket with no compliant expansion like the peritoneum.

The spatial pattern is key. **Retroperitoneal bleeding tracks along the psoas margin and distorts the renal outline**, not the free-flowing, shifting dullness of intraperitoneal blood. On CT, that blood is **rounded and contained by the fatty retroperitoneal fascia**, unlike the crescentic, layered look of a perinephric hematoma from a simple contusion.

So for this patient, **a flank ecchymosis (Grey Turner sign) would be expected**, not diffuse abdominal tenderness. The bedside decision: **if unstable, this needs angioembolization, not laparotomy** — because the bleeding is behind the peritoneum, not into the gut.
